strengths: The physically informed residual formulation using the zeroth-step Hamiltonian as both an input descriptor and an output prior is sensible and practically relevant; it substantially reduces the target's numerical range.

The work tackles an important and difficult problem and combines equivariant modeling, reciprocal-space supervision, SOC-aware Hamiltonians, and a potentially valuable 17,000-structure dataset covering 68 elements.

The paper includes component-wise ablations for the input prior, residual target, TraceGrad mechanism, distance-partitioned models, and reciprocal-space losses. The full method obtains the best reported real-space Gauge MAE.
End-to-end timing includes construction of the zeroth-step Hamiltonian, and the CPU as well as GPU measurements indicate a meaningful reduction relative to the reported self-consistent DFT workflow.
weaknesses: The empirical study contains no comparison with existing Hamiltonian-prediction methods such as DeepH-2, QHNet, or other relevant baselines trained on the proposed dataset. Comparisons only against the authors' own ablations cannot establish competitiveness or state-of-the-art performance.

The central claims of universality and generalization are not adequately tested. The data are randomly split from the same Materials Project sample, with no composition-, prototype-, element-, or distribution-held-out evaluation and no analysis of near-duplicate structures across splits. Element-wise errors on overlapping elements do not demonstrate out-of-distribution generalization.

Downstream accuracy is evaluated mainly through selected band-structure plots. The paper lacks test-set-wide quantitative metrics for band energies, gaps, Fermi-level states, eigenvectors, or ghost-state frequency. Consequently, the strong claims of DFT-level precision and elimination of ghost states are insufficiently supported and may reflect favorable example selection.

The reported sub-microelectronvolt accuracy of spin-off-diagonal blocks is misleading as evidence of learned SOC accuracy: the zeroth-step Hamiltonian already differs from the target by less than 0.001 meV in these blocks. The model is therefore not shown to learn a substantial SOC correction, and no SOC-sensitive observable or challenging heavy-element subset is evaluated.

There is a mathematical inconsistency in Eq. (20): after defining the trace as tr(Delta H_gt Delta H_gt^dagger), the expanded second factor is written as (Delta H_gt-H^(0))^dagger, which is not equivalent. The description of the 256-dimensional TraceGrad feature and the expression f + partial z/partial f also leave dimensional and implementation details unclear.

Reproducibility is incomplete: there is no accessible code/data link or release and license statement, while essential details such as batching, sampled k-points, exact attention equations, parameter counts, training time, and preprocessing are missing. Results use only one random seed and provide no uncertainty estimates.

The four distance-specialized models have greater aggregate capacity and compute than the single-network ablation, so the claimed benefit of the 'ensemble' is confounded by model size. Likewise, no matched-capacity baseline jointly removes both the zeroth-step input and residual output prior.

The dataset is restricted to nonmagnetic compounds, omits major element families, and uses one fixed functional, basis, pseudopotential family, and electronic-structure code. A fixed 6x6x6 k-point mesh is also used across cells of differing dimensions without a convergence study. These limitations conflict with the broad 'universal' and high-quality-ground-truth claims.

The efficiency comparison is not accompanied by accuracy-runtime tradeoffs or comparisons with learned baselines, and the largest tested systems are small enough that the claimed near-linear large-system scaling is extrapolated rather than demonstrated.

strengths: Using the zeroth-step Hamiltonian as both a physically informed input and a residual-prediction anchor is sensible and practically useful; the ablations suggest that both choices improve real-space error.
The proposed benchmark is potentially valuable: it contains 17,000 SOC-enabled calculations, covers 68 elements, and uses relatively rich numerical atomic-orbital bases.
The paper combines equivariant modeling, reciprocal-space supervision, and distance-specialized predictors into a coherent framework, with implementation details and component-wise ablations.
The end-to-end timing study includes the cost of constructing the zeroth-step Hamiltonian and indicates a substantial speed advantage over self-consistent DFT on the tested systems.
weaknesses: The empirical study contains no competitive learned baseline. NextHAM is compared only with the zeroth-step Hamiltonian and its own ablations, despite discussing DeepH-2 and other universal/SOC Hamiltonian models. Consequently, the paper does not establish an advance over the state of the art.

The central claim of universal generalization is unsupported. The train, validation, and test structures are randomly sampled from the same Materials Project population; there are no element-disjoint, composition-disjoint, prototype-disjoint, temporal, or genuinely out-of-distribution tests. Per-element errors on overlapping subsets do not measure generalization to unseen chemistry.

Band-structure quality is shown only through selected qualitative plots. There are no aggregate band-energy, eigenvector, band-gap, Fermi-surface, or ghost-state metrics over the full test set, nor a stated sample-selection protocol. Claims of DFT-level accuracy and elimination of ghost states are therefore substantially stronger than the evidence.

The reported sub-microelectronvolt SOC-block result is misleading as evidence for the neural method: Table 1 shows that the zeroth-step Hamiltonian already has sub-microelectronvolt error in those blocks. The meaningful overall improvement is from 2.606 to 1.417 meV, and its significance cannot be judged without external baselines or uncertainty estimates.

The loss derivation appears technically inconsistent. Because the balancing ratio in the trace term is stop-gradient, equality of the combined loss value to the Hamiltonian loss does not imply equality of gradients with respect to the gauge shift. Thus the claim that the trace term can be omitted when analytically deriving the optimal gauge parameter is not justified. Equation 20 also appears malformed, using inconsistent factors in the trace expression.

Several technical claims are imprecise or overstated. Residual prediction reduces target magnitude or complexity, not its dimensionality; linear-time sparse eigensolution is not generally guaranteed; and the perturbation bound and its connection to the specific observed ghost states are asserted without a careful derivation or quantitative validation.

The efficiency comparison uses four A800 GPUs for the main accelerated setting and does not compare against optimized competing ML methods. It also evaluates only the dataset's mostly small cells, while extrapolating favorable scaling to substantially larger systems without experiments.

Reproducibility is inadequate for a dataset-and-system contribution. The submission gives no accessible code or dataset artifact, exact Materials Project identifiers and split lists, detailed sampling procedure, sampled k-points used during training, parameter counts, memory/training costs, or multiple-seed results. Fixing one seed does not quantify variability.

The scope excludes magnetic materials even though the paper repeatedly uses broad language such as universal and spanning real-world materials. This is a substantial limitation for a SOC-focused Hamiltonian model and is not adequately reflected in the claims.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and computationally demanding problem, and the combination of a predictive method with a 17,000-structure Hamiltonian dataset spanning 68 elements, SOC, and relatively rich orbital bases could be a valuable community contribution.

Using the zeroth-step Hamiltonian as both a physically informed input and an output prior is intuitive and practically effective: the reported ablation increases Gauge MAE from 1.417 to 1.720 meV without the input prior and to 2.974 meV without residual prediction.

The architecture combines E(3)-equivariant attention, persistent edge representations, TraceGrad, and distance-specialized submodels in a technically coherent framework suited to pairwise Hamiltonian prediction.

The reciprocal-space objective addresses an important failure mode that real-space elementwise errors can overlook. Ablations of the k-space and cross-subspace losses, accompanied by band-structure examples exhibiting ghost states, provide useful evidence for the design.

The paper reports substantial end-to-end acceleration over self-consistent DFT while including the cost of constructing the zeroth-step Hamiltonian, rather than reporting neural-network inference alone.
The manuscript provides extensive implementation, DFT, dataset, runtime, and component-ablation details, and the presentation and figures are generally clear.
weaknesses: The central experimental weakness is the absence of comparisons against existing Hamiltonian-learning systems such as DeepH-E3, QHNet, DeepH-2, or the cited universal SOC model. Component ablations do not establish whether NextHAM advances the state of the art, making the claimed superiority and top-tier significance difficult to assess.

The claimed universal generalization is evaluated only through a random IID split of Materials Project structures. There are no composition-disjoint, element-holdout, prototype-disjoint, out-of-distribution, external-dataset, or substantially larger-system tests. Closely related compositions or structures may therefore occur across splits.

Band-structure quality is supported mainly by selected qualitative plots. The paper should report test-set-wide quantitative errors for band energies, gaps, Fermi-level properties, eigenvectors, and ghost-state frequency, ideally against competing methods. The statement that the predictions attain DFT-level accuracy is stronger than the current evidence.

The dataset is restricted to nonmagnetic compounds, even though magnetism is an important regime for SOC Hamiltonians. Moreover, the advertised sub-micro-eV spin-off-diagonal accuracy largely reflects that the zeroth-step Hamiltonian already differs from the target by less than 0.001 meV in those blocks, rather than demonstrating a difficult learned prediction.

Novelty is somewhat incremental at the architectural level: the method extends previously proposed TraceGrad and equivariant attention, adds residual learning from a DFT initialization, and uses an ensemble. The paper does not sufficiently distinguish these choices experimentally from strong prior architectures.

Residual prediction reduces the numerical range of the target but does not reduce its dimensionality, contrary to repeated claims in the manuscript. Related claims about simplifying the output space should be stated more precisely.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: no accessible code or dataset artifact is identified, model parameter counts and training cost are omitted, and results use only one fixed random seed without uncertainty estimates. The four-model ensemble also raises compute and fairness questions that should be addressed in baseline comparisons.

The assertion of strict E(3) equivariance is not backed by numerical equivariance tests, and some architectural details needed to independently reconstruct the attention and TraceGrad integration are left at a high level.

Overall, the work is promising and close to the acceptance boundary, but the missing state-of-the-art baselines and limited IID-only evaluation are substantial evidence gaps for a top-tier acceptance decision.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and difficult problem and combines several meaningful ideas: zeroth-step Hamiltonians as physics-informed inputs, residual Hamiltonian prediction, an E(3)-equivariant Transformer, and reciprocal-space supervision.
Materials-HAM-SOC is potentially a valuable contribution: it contains 17,000 SOC-aware calculations, covers more than 60 elements, and uses relatively rich atomic-orbital bases.
The reported accuracy is strong. NextHAM obtains 1.417 meV Gauge MAE, substantially outperforming the adapted DeepH-E3 baseline, and the component ablations consistently favor the full model.

The paper evaluates more than matrix-element error: it presents band structures, optical conductivity, SOC-resolved errors, and end-to-end runtime measurements that include construction of the zeroth-step Hamiltonian.
The manuscript is generally clear and provides extensive appendices describing symmetry machinery, DFT settings, loss terms, architecture, ablations, and efficiency.
weaknesses: The central claim of universal or out-of-distribution generalization is insufficiently supported. The main split is random, with no analysis of composition or structural-family leakage, while unseen-element generalization is demonstrated using only one Ne-containing test structure. This is far too limited to establish extrapolation across elements.

Evaluation of downstream physical fidelity is predominantly qualitative and based on selected examples. The paper does not report aggregate band-energy errors, eigenvector or observable errors, ghost-state frequency, or uncertainty across the full test set. Consequently, the claim that the reciprocal-space objective eliminates ghost states is stronger than the evidence.

The broad-coverage benchmark comparison is limited to one adapted DeepH-E3 baseline that reportedly fails to converge well. Its tuning, parameter count, compute budget, and convergence behavior are not documented sufficiently. Comparisons to additional modern Hamiltonian predictors and capacity-matched baselines are needed.

There is a mathematical ambiguity in the gauge-aware objective. The paper argues that the trace-balanced loss is numerically equal to the Hamiltonian loss and therefore omits the trace term when deriving the optimal gauge parameter. However, the stop-gradient coefficient makes their derivatives different, while the trace target itself depends on the gauge. Thus the stated closed-form minimizer is not clearly the minimizer of the implemented training objective. Equation 24 also appears internally inconsistent in its definition of the residual trace target.

The strongest SOC result is potentially misleading: the spin-off-diagonal and relevant imaginary components are already below the reporting resolution in the zeroth-step Hamiltonian, so their sub-micro-eV error does not demonstrate that the learned correction accurately models SOC effects. The dataset is also restricted to nonmagnetic materials.

Statistical reliability is weak: all training and evaluation use a single random seed, with no error bars or repeated splits. Dataset identifiers, exact split manifests, model size, total training cost, and several implementation details are absent, limiting reproducibility.

The efficiency experiment uses four A800 GPUs for NextHAM versus four CPU cores for DFT, so the headline speedup is not a resource-matched comparison. Large-system scaling is asserted theoretically but not measured, and dependence on an ABACUS-specific zeroth-step calculation limits the claimed universality.

strengths: The zeroth-step Hamiltonian is a physically motivated input and residual-learning target that substantially reduces the regression burden.
Joint real-space and reciprocal-space supervision addresses an important practical failure mode—ghost states—and the qualitative band-structure and optical-conductivity examples are promising.
Materials-HAM-SOC is potentially valuable: it contains 17,000 periodic structures, broad elemental coverage, relatively rich orbital bases, and explicit spin–orbit coupling.
The paper includes component ablations and reports end-to-end timing that includes construction of the zeroth-step Hamiltonian.
weaknesses: The evidence does not support the central claims of universality or DFT-level fidelity. Evaluation is predominantly a random in-distribution split of nonmagnetic Materials Project crystals using one DFT setup. The only element-level out-of-distribution result is a single Ne-containing structure; there are no systematic leave-elements-, compositions-, prototypes-, or structure-families-out tests.

Downstream accuracy is evaluated mainly through selected visual examples. The paper lacks test-set-wide quantitative band-energy, eigenvector, optical-property, topology, and ghost-state metrics. Consequently, claims such as preserving band topology and nearly eliminating ghost states are not established.

The main broad-dataset baseline is only DeepH-E3, which reportedly fails to converge. Comparisons with stronger or more recent approaches discussed in the related work are absent, while baseline tuning, parameter counts, compute budgets, and convergence diagnostics are not provided. This makes the large reported advantage difficult to interpret.

The SOC result is misleadingly emphasized: the spin-off-diagonal and imaginary components are already below the reporting precision for the zeroth-step Hamiltonian, and the correction network primarily learns the real spin-conserving block. Thus the claimed sub-micro-eV SOC prediction is not compelling evidence of learned accuracy.

Several ablations are confounded. In particular, the full method uses four distance-specialized models whereas the ensemble ablation uses one model, so the improvement may simply reflect greater parameter and compute capacity. Results are reported for a single fixed seed without uncertainty or statistical tests.

The reciprocal-space objective is insufficiently validated. Its mathematical presentation contains ambiguities around differentiating the adaptively normalized trace loss and analytically selecting the gauge parameter, while the asserted connection between the PQ penalty, ghost states, and topology is supported only by hand-selected plots.

Reproducibility is currently inadequate: the code, model, dataset, and extraction links in the reproducibility statement are blank. Important details such as parameter counts, training cost, exact sampling of k-points, dataset filtering and deduplication, sample-level error distributions, and baseline configurations are missing.

The efficiency experiment uses four A800 GPUs for NextHAM GPU inference versus four CPU cores for DFT and contains no large-system scaling experiment. It therefore supports a workflow-specific wall-clock improvement, but not the stronger asymptotic and broad efficiency claims.

Overall, the idea and dataset are promising, but the missing releases, weak and potentially unfair baseline coverage, narrow generalization study, and lack of aggregate downstream validation are major shortcomings for a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and difficult problem: accurate, transferable Hamiltonian prediction for chemically diverse periodic materials with spin-orbit coupling.

Using the inexpensive zeroth-step Hamiltonian as a physically informed input and learning only its residual correction is well motivated. The ablations indicate substantial benefits from both choices.

The E(3)-equivariant Transformer, TraceGrad mechanism, and reciprocal-space subspace losses form a coherent framework. The explicit penalty on low-/high-energy subspace coupling is physically meaningful.

Materials-HAM-SOC is potentially a valuable contribution: it contains 17,000 structures, more than 60 elements, SOC, and relatively rich orbital bases. The DFT settings and dataset statistics are documented in considerable detail.

The reported results are promising: NextHAM obtains 1.417 meV Gauge MAE, substantially outperforms the adapted DeepH-E3 baseline, improves over DeepH-E3 and TraceGrad on two specialized datasets, and shows consistent gains in component ablations.
The runtime comparison includes zeroth-step Hamiltonian construction and reports both CPU and GPU inference, showing a large end-to-end speed advantage over the self-consistent DFT workflow.
weaknesses: The claimed universal and out-of-distribution generalization is not convincingly established. The main evaluation uses a random structure split, while element-level extrapolation is demonstrated using only one Ne-containing test structure. Composition-, prototype-, element-, and size-disjoint evaluations are needed, and magnetic materials are excluded.

A central claim is that the reciprocal-space objective suppresses ghost states and preserves downstream physics, but the evidence is mostly selected qualitative band plots and one optical-conductivity example. There are no test-set-level band-energy errors, ghost-state frequencies, wavefunction metrics, topology checks, or quantitative downstream-property statistics.

The main benchmark comparison is limited to an adapted DeepH-E3 model. Comparisons against more recent universal Hamiltonian approaches, DeepH-2-style architectures, and simpler strong residual-learning baselines are missing. The ensemble ablation also changes model capacity, so it does not isolate specialization from parameter count.

Several claims are overstated. A 1.417 meV matrix-element error is called DFT-level accuracy without comparison to DFT numerical variability or application-specific tolerances, while the sub-micro-eV spin-off-diagonal result is largely inherited from the already highly accurate zeroth-step Hamiltonian. Likewise, preserving band topology is asserted but never evaluated.

The method description does not provide sufficient equations for the proposed equivariant attention, normalization, and feed-forward operations to independently verify the strict E(3)-symmetry claim. There are also confusing or inconsistent expressions in the trace-target definition and overly broad statements that adding a gauge shift leaves all downstream quantities unchanged, even though it shifts generalized eigenvalues.

Reproducibility is presently limited: the stated code, pretrained-model, dataset, and extraction-code links are absent in the manuscript; parameter counts, training time, memory requirements, and multi-seed uncertainty are not reported.

The scalability argument is extrapolated from a test set containing few large systems. Large-system accuracy and empirical scaling are not demonstrated, and the four-submodel ensemble may impose substantial training and deployment costs that are not quantified.
